scenes.title: Today's view dissolves into the past

scenes.caption: Photo 1850
scenes.text: Each side of the iwan is framed with a 33-metre (108 ft) high pishtaq (vaulted archway) with two similarly shaped arched balconies stacked on either side.

scenes.caption: Photo 1850
scenes.text: The base structure is a large multi-chambered cube with chamfered corners forming an eight-sided structure that is approximately 57.3 metres (188 ft) long on each of the four long sides.

scenes.caption: Photo 1850
scenes.text: The entire complex sits on a platform measuring 300 metres (980 ft) in length and 8.7 metres (28.5 ft) in height on the banks of the Yamuna river.

scenes.caption: Photo 1850
scenes.text: It was commissioned in 1631 by the fifth Mughal emperor, Shah Jahan (r. 1628–1658), to house the tomb of his late wife, Mumtaz Mahal; it also houses the tomb of Shah Jahan himself.

scenes.caption: Photo 1850
scenes.text: The cenotaphs were originally covered by a screen made of gold on the occasion of the second anniversary of Mumtaz Mahal's death in 1633, which was later replaced by the marble screen in 1643.

scenes.caption: Photo 1860
scenes.text: Abdul Hamid Lahori, in his 1636 book Padshahnama, refers to the Taj Mahal as rauza-i munawwara (Perso-Arabic: روضه منواره, rawdah-i munawwarah), meaning the illumined or illustrious tomb.

scenes.caption: Photo 1862
scenes.text: Construction of the mausoleum was completed in 1648, although work on other parts of the complex continued for another five years.

scenes.caption: Photo 1862
scenes.text: The Taj Mahal was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983 for being "the jewel of Muslim art in India and one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage".

scenes.caption: Photo 1862
scenes.text: In 2007, it was declared a winner of the New 7 Wonders of the World initiative.

scenes.title: The place
scenes.text: A mausoleum commissioned by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, built from 1632 to 1653. Photographed from the 1850s by John Murray, then Samuel Bourne and Lala Deen Dayal.
